Quirky T-19A Kestrel Beats the B-21 Raider Nuclear Bomber in Becoming USAF's Newest Airplane
7 photos
Photo: USAF
In the military world, new aircraft types don't come along very often. Sure, you could argue that new planes are revealed all the time, but that mostly happens because much older platforms are being modernized and upgraded to fulfil new roles. When it comes to an aircraft type that hasn't been used before, as said, they don't come along very often.
When it comes to the American Air Force , the eyes of the world are affixed to the upcoming B-21 Raider nuclear bomber and the F-47 sixth-generation fighter, but those are still a long way from being ready to join the fleet as the newest aircraft around. Until that happens, a new kind of airplane entered the scene.
They call it the T-19A Kestrel, the work of Arkansas-based Game Aerospace, and it has been created with a specific goal in mind: to serve the needs of the U.S. Air Force Academy by training some of its pilots in the art of aerobatics.
That's right, aerobatics, because the Academy is now actively pursuing the creation of a national aerobatic and demonstration team. It needs that not only to wow the crowds, but also to get greater cadet involvement in training, demonstrations, and program operations.
The Kestrel, named so in honor of the small predatory bird of the falcon family, is based on the GB1 GameBird, an aerobatic aircraft that first flew a little more than a decade ago, adapted for the use of the Air Force in just ten months of work.
The plane is a tandem-seater, but as small as you'd expect: it only stands 25 feet (7.7 meters) from wing tip to wing tip, and 23 feet (seven meters) from nose to tail. Powering it is a Lycoming six-cylinder piston engine rated at 303 horsepower, which is enough to give it a top speed of 230 mph (370 kph).
The plane officially entered service with the Academy at the end of last week, when the Kestrel debuted as part of a flyover of the Cadet Wing’s noon meal formation. For all intents and purposes, this is the first powered aerobatic aircraft fielded by the Academy.
The organization had four of these things built, and it will use them to give cadets more flight time and aerobatic experience as they seek to enter the Air Force or Undergraduate Pilot Training.
Getting to it using these machines will be six active-duty military pilots from the Academy staff, who, together with the 306th Flying Training Group, will form the initial cadre. These pilots have been tasked with creating and executing an aerobatic training curriculum.
For the moment, these six will also become the primary demonstration pilots, whom we'll probably see soon enough at recruiting events and air shows across the nation.
